source.title: L2CEval: Evaluating Language-to-Code Generation Capabilities of Large Language Models
source.authors: Ansong Ni; Peng-Cheng Yin; Yilun Zhao; Martin Riddell; Troy Feng; Rui Shen; Stephen Yin; Ye Liu; Semih Yavuz; Cai-Ming Xiong; Shafiq R. Joty; Yingbo Zhou; Dragomir R. Radev; Arman Cohan

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream execution accuracy across models of different sizes and plots performance against pretraining tokens and compute. This bears on downstream scaling, but it does not use held-out cross-entropy loss or fit the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The scaling results are task execution-accuracy comparisons, not held-out pretraining loss. The study does not fit power laws, test forecasts from small runs, or identify compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its architecture comparisons do not hold parameter count fixed. Prompt-exemplar sensitivity and instruction-tuning results are outside these claim versions. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates 54 existing models on language-to-code tasks and relates execution accuracy to model size, pretraining tokens and estimated compute. This bears on V6, downstream improvement with scale, in a new setting. It fits no loss curves, makes no forecasts and compares no compute-optimal splits. Comparisons span model families with confounded data, architecture and objectives.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find larger models generally better on all tasks, with smoother scaling on programming-like tasks and more emergent scaling on reasoning tasks. More tokens help similar-sized models, consistent with Kaplan et al. Some models (InCoder-6B, CodeGen-16B) appear under-trained. Training on code tokens is more compute-efficient for L2C tasks. The authors caution that confounds between model families limit these conclusions.
record.recipe_differences: Measures downstream execution accuracy on language-to-code tasks across existing models rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss in controlled training runs; it does not fit power laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed size-scaling trend differs by task: it is described as smoother for Spider and MBPP and more emergent for WikiTQ and GSM8k.
record.peer_reviewed: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The comparisons span models with confounding differences such as training data, architecture, and pretraining objective; the authors explicitly caution that these factors limit conclusions. Proprietary model details are incomplete. The scaling results use downstream execution accuracy rather than pretraining loss, and the relevant plots do not provide numerical point values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling results were left out. Results on instruction tuning, prompt sensitivity, calibration, and data mixture were not extracted because they do not directly measure the scaling behavior named in the tested version.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No prediction of downstream accuracy from pretraining loss, and no quantitative fit or forecast of task scaling.
No fitting choices or exponents are examined.

missing.what: Within-series numeric size-scaling values, e.g. Pythia 1.4/6.9/12B Spider 5.7/12.5/16.2 and LLaMA-2 7/13/70B Spider 21.7/35.7/58.5. Also the non-monotonic cases: Vicuna-13B vs 33B on GSM8k; dolly-v2-7B vs 12B on MBPP; LLaMA-2-13B vs 70B on MBPP.
Mean win rate by size group: <2B models 5–33%, 20–100B models 70–88%.

record.verdict_notes: All scaling evidence comes from heterogeneous off-the-shelf models, not controlled runs. Table 3 and Table 7 disagree on LLaMA-2-70B MBPP (36.8 vs 26.6). Spider correct programs include about 7% spurious ones. Instruction tuning, prompt sensitivity and calibration results do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Forecasting larger-run held-out loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token split at fixed compute, its scaling with compute, and comparisons between parameter and token growth rates.
Isolating architecture details at fixed parameter count and measuring their effect on loss.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study reports downstream execution accuracy trends but does not predict task performance from pretraining loss or provide a quantitative predictive scaling fit.

The study notes comparison confounds and variation across tasks, but does not test sensitivity of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits to fitting choices, nor test whether loss curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: selected models (average execution accuracy across selected tasks)
rows.operation_detail: Plotted average task performance against the number of pretraining tokens seen.
rows.value: Models trained with more tokens generally perform better on L2C tasks when comparing similar-sized models.
rows.note: The plotted points are individual models, while the reported performance measure averages across the four named tasks. The text gives a general trend, not numerical point values.
rows.check: Among similar-sized models, more training tokens generally helps (e.g. CodeGen-16B vs StarCoder-15.5B). The comparison is across model families, so it is confounded.

rows.subject: selected models (average execution accuracy across selected tasks)
rows.operation_detail: Plotted average task performance against estimated pretraining compute.
rows.value: The text says the plot suggests code-specific models are more compute-efficient for L2C tasks than general LLMs; the dashed line separates the groups.
rows.note: The plotted points are individual models, while the reported performance measure averages across the four named tasks. The text states a group-level trend but gives no numerical point values.
rows.check: Performance against compute splits into two groups by data type (code-specific vs general), so compute alone does not predict L2C performance. Some models are flagged as under-trained.

relationships.condition: Programming-oriented tasks (Spider, MBPP), and token count among similar-sized models
relationships.reason: The authors describe execution accuracy rising relatively smoothly with size on Spider and MBPP (R1, R4). More pretraining tokens generally improve similar-sized models (R5).
relationships.display_finding: Execution accuracy increased relatively smoothly with size on Spider and MBPP, while more pretraining tokens generally improved similarly sized models.

relationships.reason: Accuracy rises with size, but the trend is described as emergent rather than smooth, so it is less predictable (R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: WikiTQ and GSM8k accuracy increased with size through patterns described as emergent rather than smooth.

relationships.condition: Performance against pretraining compute across data mixtures
relationships.reason: Code-specific and general models fall on separate sides of the compute-performance plot, so compute alone does not predict accuracy; the data mix matters (R6).
relationships.display_finding: Code-specific and general models occupied different compute–performance relationships, making data mixture necessary to interpret accuracy.

relationships.condition: Within-series size comparisons in Table 7 (from the text, not rows)
relationships.reason: Several larger models score below their smaller sibling, e.g. Vicuna-33B 4.8 vs Vicuna-13B 18.1 on GSM8k. Other cases: dolly-v2-12B 3.8 vs dolly-v2-7B 12.0 on MBPP, and LLaMA-2-70B 26.6 vs LLaMA-2-13B 27.0 on MBPP. No row records these.
relationships.display_finding: Vicuna-33B scored 4.8 versus 13B's 18.1 on GSM8k, dolly-v2-12B scored 3.8 versus 7B's 12.0 on MBPP, and LLaMA-2-70B scored 26.6 versus 13B's 27.0 on MBPP.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
